DOM&NIC: "At its heart, the story is about determination, resilience, and the refusal to give up and we wanted to bring the audience along on that journey in the most entertaining, cinematic and emotionally involving way possible. "We wanted the audience to empathize with the bird as a character, but never lose the sense that this is a real bird in a real cage." "The animation had to stay grounded in behavior that felt believable and true to life, so the audience could enjoy the fantasy while also feeling it could really happen. "A particular challenge was creating seamless transitions between open and folded wings, solved through complex simulation that allowed the feathers to fold naturally into one another."

records.description: ETC director Michael ‘Chappers' Chapman leans into his background in CG and love of technical illustration to deconstruct the new Lexus R3 electric SUV in obsessive detail while maintaining a sense of aspirational elegance. Michael ‘Chappers' Chapman: "I wanted the film to be grounded in the real world: fantastical elements juxtaposed with believability. "Most importantly – the RZ needed to remain a tangible, sellable asset. We scoured over 300 locations across Europe to get it right, casting actors who brought an easy elegance and charm. "Ahead of the shoot, we worked on storyboards, first creating a board-o-matic for timing, and then moving into a world where I'm most comfortable – Pre-viz – to illustrate the intention of each shot. "The movements needed to feel elegant and the transitions seamless, so we recced the real environment which allowed us to bring it into 3D and test out camera moves accurately pre-shoot. "Having a clear plan helped streamline communication with cast and crew on set (and helped my anxiety not spike on my health tracker). "Pre my career in VFX & CG, I did a degree in technical illustration. So, the mention of macro scenes and exploded views are akin to mentioning ice cream to a child in the height of summer. "The challenge was to produce a film that mirrored the craft of the vehicle itself. Effortlessly poised, blending live action and VFX in a totally seamless way. Just how deconstructed should we go, whilst ensuring it wasn't visually noisy? "This led us to the use of parallax. We minimized the perceived animated movement between parts, instead using the movement of the camera to expand and contract the car. Each shot required layering – whether it being live action, full CG, or a bit of both. "We also worked on set extension, cleanup, CG environment enhancement, as well as beauty work to the car itself, ensuring perfect matches for true authenticity. "Finally, we finessed the edit and graded the live action and CG shots together, which helped bring harmony to a really special film."

records.description: Brad Smith, producer at Magna Studios in Los Angeles: "Channel 4 approached Magna to collaborate with Deadhorses (James Topley and Ivo Beckett), to create a film in the duo's distinctive visual style. "The ambition was to create a trailer that captures the raw, unfiltered grit of the Women's FA Cup, with no gloss and no sugar coating. "It leans into the passion, chaos, and spectacle of grassroots football, brought to life through Deadhorse's signature aesthetic of controlled visual disorder. "The main creative challenge was balancing a raw, grungy look in a way that would still meet the requirements for television broadcast. It became a careful balancing act for both the Channel 4 creatives and Deadhorses. "The film is built from archive material and footage captured at live games using mixed media, including an Arri SR2, Bolex, Canon XL1, Kodak FunSavers, iPhones, and Sony Handycam. "One of the biggest challenges, beyond blending these different formats together, was capturing the intensity of a live game on film. "Overall, the project ran for over three months, with one shoot in January, another in February, and post-production continuing through to mid-March. "For the ball-on-fire shot, we had to build a fake pitch in the car park at Dulwich Hamlet FC. It was surprisingly difficult and time-consuming, especially given we were constructing it right next to an actual football field."

records.description: Marie Vaillant, producer at Mathematic in Paris: "Finch wanted its very first brand campaign to feel radically different from traditional wellness advertising. "Instead of presenting an idealized or overly polished version of self-care, the goal was to create something emotionally honest, funny, strange, and deeply human — inspired by the real rituals people rely on to get through the day. "The project embraced specificity, vulnerability, absurd humour, and warmth all at once, while remaining emotionally sincere and relatable. "One big creative challenge was finding the right balance between emotional honesty and absurd comedy. "The film constantly shifts between grounded moments and surreal situations, so every sequence needed to feel expressive and handcrafted without losing emotional authenticity. "Another challenge was preserving spontaneity and humanity throughout the visuals. We intentionally avoided an overly polished aesthetic to maintain the film's warmth and personality. "The entire film was crafted fully by hand with no AI involvement, which required a very collaborative and precise pipeline across all departments. "Mathematic handled the complete fabrication of the film, including character animation, environments, lighting, FX, rendering, and compositing. "The production followed a fully digital animation pipeline. Early storyboards and animatics were developed in Photoshop before moving into full CG production. "Mathematic created the 3D animation and environments in Maya, while final compositing and finishing were completed in Flame. "At a moment where many productions increasingly rely on generative workflows and automation, the team chose to animate and fabricate every frame manually. "This human approach became central to the emotional quality of the film. The subtle imperfections, expressive performances, and tactile feeling of the animation all come directly from artists crafting the work by hand. "Kirsten Lepore's sensibility also played a huge role in shaping the tone of the project, blending emotional vulnerability, absurd humour, and visual experimentation in a way that immediately resonated with the entire team."

records.description: The non-playable characters of the gaming world finally have their day as one of them breaks free in this Coinbase spot by MJZ director Oscar Hudson, which aired during the Academy Awards. Instead of replicating the low-poly look of the retro gaming characters in 3D, Hudson chose to suit up actors in highly convincing costumes and work with French choreographer Maeva Berthelot to refine their quirky motion and walk cycles. Toby Treyer-Evans, founder at Isle of Any: "It felt important to allow the viewer to see themselves as that player in the middle of the screen. "We wanted it to feel like a nod to the old world of video games, representing an old system, but also modern enough that you could relate to it in today's world. "The attention to detail from a production perspective was incredible. "Every suit button, lapel, and texture was 2D printed directly onto the suits; the sets were printed in a pixelated way, and each actor was trained to walk like a game character. "It led to a world that felt entirely like a game, but with real humans walking around."

records.description: Mikołaj Błoński, Managing Director & EP at BluBlu Studios in Kraków, Poland: "WWF needed a hero film for their Nature Needs Us Now campaign, an urgent public call to action around nature conservation. "The brief was built around a poem written and performed by WWF-US CEO Carter Roberts, which gave the project an unusually personal foundation from the start. "The studio was given creative latitude to find an artistic form that matched the sincerity and emotional directness of the text. "The central challenge was honouring the intimacy of Carter Roberts' voice and words without over-producing the piece. "The temptation in campaign work is to reach for polish, but here, restraint was the craft. The team needed to find an aesthetic that felt genuinely human and tactile, not decorative. "Working with London-based director Natasza Cetner, whose process centres on pencil and crayon drawings on paper, helped anchor that instinct. "Protecting the analogue quality throughout the production pipeline — from scan to final delivery — without losing the texture and imperfection that made it work, required constant editorial discipline. "We wouldn't frame this as a technical challenge, but finding the right medium to carry this particular message was a genuinely interesting creative exercise. "In an era increasingly saturated with AI-generated visuals, the choice to work with pencil and crayon on paper felt both deliberate and necessary. "The analogue process isn't a stylistic flourish here, it's the argument. The imperfections, the texture, and the hand of the artist are precisely what give the film its credibility and emotional weight. "The music, composed by Jakub Tokarczyk and built around kalimba, woodblocks, and shakers, was chosen specifically to stay in the same register as the visuals: grounded, natural, unforced. The film is designed to be felt as much as watched."

records.description: Ambrogio Bergamaschi, creative lead at Found in London: "The brief was deceptively simple: launch a nearly invisible hearing aid for Specsavers in a way that would genuinely capture attention. "The real challenge wasn't functional; it was cultural. Hearing aids are often marketed in a clinical way, which can unintentionally reinforce stigma. "The ambition was to reframe the device as something desirable and intimate, positioning it not as a medical necessity, but as a catalyst for connection. "Golin London approached us with a tongue-in-cheek concept: present the hearing aid as ‘the device your relationship has been missing', a couple's connection device. "The idea stemmed from a strong writing-led insight that connection sits at the heart of both relationships and hearing. "By leaning into ambiguity and borrowing the visual language of a different category, we could intrigue audiences and play with perception before revealing the truth. "The film was to be fully realised in 3D, with slow, deliberate movement, sensual lighting, and tactile materials to create an intimate arena. "Voiceover would play a central role in reinforcing the connection narrative, while the visuals were crafted to keep the audience guessing. "On paper, it was a simple brief. In execution, it required nuance, something provocative enough to spark conversation, yet art-directed with taste and restraint to feel elevated rather than sensational. "The biggest creative challenge was striking the right balance between suggestion and reveal. "The entire idea depended on ambiguity, showing just enough to spark a specific assumption, but never so much that the illusion collapsed too early. "It required constant calibration: build intrigue, keep it tasteful, and don't give the game away. "It was about holding the entire piece together: the edit, the pacing, the music, the voiceover. Every element needed to pull in the same direction. "Technically, the piece wasn't about complexity; it was about consistency. We worked across multiple lighting setups while maintaining a single, coherent visual language. "The cinematography had to feel intimate and sculpted, yet still believable. Holding that tone across different environments required precision and restraint. "On a project like this, subtlety is the technical challenge. The craft has to disappear so the audience stays immersed in the story. "One of the most surprisingly difficult decisions was choosing the music as the piece's mood shifted dramatically depending on the track. "In early edit tests, we paired the film with an '80s-style jazzy bass track. It pushed the tone so far into cheeky territory that everyone internally couldn't stop laughing. "It was a sharp reminder of how much perception is shaped by sound, and how a single musical choice can completely reframe an audience's interpretation." Schedule: Six weeks.

records.description: Álvaro Ibáñez, project manager at Kutuko Studio in Madrid: "Xiaomi came to us with a beautiful idea: dust bunnies. "They were clear from the start that they wanted to communicate the product from an emotional and accessible angle, not through the typical tech-heavy messaging. "From there, our job was to take that spark and turn it into a full story. "We shaped the narrative, built the arc, the tone, and that little love story that turns two balls of dust into soulful protagonists… without giving them eyes or turning them into cartoon characters. "The biggest challenge was telling a lot in a very short amount of time. We wanted the audience to connect with the dust bunnies within seconds. "We also had to find a delicate balance: making the bunnies realistic, with texture and weight, but still adorable and emotional, without falling into classic character anthropomorphization. "Achieving that emotional realism was a huge challenge. Dust bunnies are chaotic masses, full of microfibers, dynamics, and complex physical behavior. "They needed to look natural, yet still readable as characters. We went through extensive R&D, grooming tests, and simulation exploration to find that exact point where they remain dust, but they express something. "From concept, narrative, animatics, lookdev, simulations, animation, to post-production, the process took four months. A very careful, handcrafted workflow with lots of iteration to match the emotional sensitivity the brand was looking for. "We worked in Cinema 4D with the Redshift render engine, which gave us great control over lighting and the fine detail of the dust bunnies. Post-production was done in DaVinci Resolve, and sound design in Ableton. "At a time when AI can generate images and videos at absurd speeds, what truly makes a difference are stories with intention, with meaning, pieces crafted with care. "That mindset, betting on narrative, on the human element, is what allows two dust bunnies to tell a story that resonates globally."

records.description: Lucas Navarro, director and co-founder at Illogic Studios in Montpellier, France: "The story of this film was to depict an animated cut-paper world set within a perfumer's workshop. "The brief was to create a film that felt both magical and photorealistic, with a sophisticated and elegant mise-en-scène. "As with every Guerlain Christmas campaign, the artistic ambition is very high, as the elegance of the brand must come through in these films. "We were immediately drawn to the concept because we knew it had the potential to become a charming and spectacular film. "Right from the start, we were aligned with the agency on how we wanted to film this miniature world: immersive camera movements, a feeling of being swept rapidly through different universes with new surprises in every scene, and above all, freshness and poetry. "We also wanted a crescendo structure: beginning very softly and growing in scale and intensity as the film unfolds. "To make Guerlain's A Tale of Wonder as spectacular as possible, we had to overcome numerous technical challenges (the number of sets, the number of characters, FX work, etc.). "The main challenge was representing paper in 3D. To achieve a truly convincing texture, we collaborated with Marvin Büte, a German CG artist passionate about origami. "He knows how to authentically reproduce the look of crumpled, slightly folded paper, imperfect, yet incredibly charming. "This was exactly what we wanted, and he amazed us with paper hummingbirds, elephants, and chameleons that looked more real than reality itself. "To elevate the entire piece, great care was given to lighting in order to create an atmosphere that is both magical and premium. "What worked particularly well was the idea of light seeming to emanate from within the animals and spreading through the paper. "The production took nearly eight months from start to finish. Early on, we agreed with the agency to work at a slower pace, allowing us to maintain a high level of quality throughout the process. "It is also important to note that, in addition to the main film, several shorter capsule films had to be delivered."

"The technical challenge was to match the look development from two different sets of software: Blender/Cycles and Cinema 4D/Redshift. records.description: Georgi Chalakov (Senior Designer) and Rebecca Scheinberg (Production Lead) at Found in London: "We were tasked with creating a series of films to highlight Bentley's three core brand pillars — Design, Craftsmanship, and Performance — showcasing both the beauty of the cars and the power beneath their refined exteriors. "The main creative challenge was using CG to capture the beauty, craftsmanship, and exceptional finish of a Bentley, especially its intricate details. "To ensure we really highlighted the time and effort that goes into manufacturing, we visited their factory to understand the process better. "We then worked to translate this into a beautiful, larger-than-life CGI world, getting up close to hero details that we would never be able to do in live action. "Our biggest technical hurdle was capturing the factory's exceptional craftsmanship, especially the embroidery process. "We spent considerable time depicting the direction of each stitch and the smoothness of every thread, ensuring their precision was clear on screen. "Another challenge was visually transforming the abstract veneer layers into the thread that begins the stitching. We aimed to show the transition from polished, glossy surfaces to soft threads in a single continuous shot, highlighting the story behind every detail. "We were inspired by the car's intricate details and wanted to bridge the real and abstract worlds in our visuals." Schedule: Eight weeks.

records.description: Martin Engh, director and co-owner of ADP in Oslo, Norway: "The brief from the agency was to tell an emotional story about a family of mice who find shelter in an empty plastic bottle. "It's a warm and cozy story until the bottle falls over and we realise that the mice won't be able to get out. This is a real problem in nature. "Initially, the challenge was convincing the client that traditional 2D cel animation still has a place in mass communication. Thankfully, the agency team at Pulse championed the vision all the way, giving us the freedom to do things the right way. "One of the biggest creative challenges was shaping the ending of the film. The story required a sudden and dramatic tonal shift, as the bottle that serves as the mice's home tips over, trapping them inside and ultimately leading to their death. "The challenge was to make this moment emotionally impactful without moving into melodrama, and to clearly communicate the outcome without explicitly showing it. "One of the technical challenges was maintaining stylistic consistency while working with a large team of background artists and animators. "Another technical challenge was defining the look of the bottle's interior, translating its roundness and distortion. "Another deliberate choice, rather than a challenge per se, was to limit the use of shadows and highlights to achieve the look of an older animated film. "Contemporary animation often relies heavily on lighting, shading, and effects, but for this project, the characters were kept relatively flat to get a classic cartoon feel. In contrast, the backgrounds were rendered with a high level of detail."

records.description: Alex Topaller and Dan Shapiro, directors/founders at Aggressive in Ridgewood, NJ: "Skoda asked us to capture their design philosophy, that form and function are inseparable, and that every detail of the car begins with people. "The brief was all about showing how real human questions and needs drive great design. "They wanted a film that felt cinematic, design-driven, and emotionally grounded. A concept car launch that blends motion typography, real voices, and striking visuals to express that dialogue between humanity and future technology. "From our first chats, we started shaping the look of the "green world," experimenting with how type could take on form and motion, and setting the tone for a story that feels alive, tactile, and unmistakably Skoda. "Our biggest challenge was keeping the typography and questions human. "It's easy for motion design to feel cold, but we wanted every word to sound like it came from a real person — a thought, a curiosity, a doubt. The type had to breathe with the voices as it sculpted the car into being. Maxim Chelyadnikov and Alex Mikhaylov, directors : "The heaviest lift was managing these insanely complex particle systems — essentially sculpting the car from living language. "Each shot involved many dynamic word particles moving in layered formations, with precise control over density, turbulence, and flow so that the typography felt organic rather than simulated. "We built the pipeline across 3ds Max, TyFlow, Houdini, and After Effects — juggling caches, data exchanges, and custom forces to keep everything art-directable. "The trick was finding that sweet spot where chaos and control coexist — letting the simulation breathe while keeping it visually legible and emotionally human. Alex Topaller: "On top of that, we didn't actually have the car. We shot a stand-in Skoda of similar proportions on the streets of Prague using a U-crane, which gave us authentic reflections, motion, and light interaction for the CG replacement. "For the interior scenes, we built a rough wooden frame that only hinted at the car's shape and shot the talent against green. It sounds primitive, but it gave us real shadows, contact points, and a sense of physicality that grounded the final CG build. "Another major challenge was designing the exact look of the transformation — how the letters become the car. "We spent a lot of time experimenting with how type morphs into sheet metal, glass, and car paint — testing particle and surface effects to make that transition feel seamless. Schedule: Two and a half months,.

records.description: Daniele Gavatorta, director at Nerdo Studio in Turin, Italy: "This project was born from a simple but powerful idea: we're all born barefoot. And being barefoot means being free – respecting the natural shape that Mother Nature gave our feet. VivoBarefoot is a bold brand that decided to team up with an equally bold agency, Thingy&Thingy, UK. They reached out with a clear statement: ‘we don't want a f**ing commercial'. "What they wanted was a manifesto, a call for change, a tool to wake people up and help them live differently. A philosophy against BigShoes: FREE Your FEET. "Our goal was to create a unique visual language, one that stayed far away from the shiny CGI worlds we usually see in big shoe brand advertising. "Instead, we wanted something imperfect, human, natural, analog. To do that, I reached out to friends and artists (mainly illustrators and animators) each with a strong handmade approach. "Techniques ranged from cut-out and collage to traditional animation and experiments with scanners to create distortions and glitches. "The result is 30 unique scenes, each completely different in style. The big challenge was making all these voices live together in one coherent flow that could still tell a story. "So a majority of pre-production focused on storyboard and animatic work, finding the best transitions and keeping the action and subject at the center. "This approach gets even trickier when you're telling a non-linear story, where each scene is more about emotions, moods, or symbolic moments rather than a straight narrative. Having a clear, big-picture vision is the first step. "Another fun challenge was that the client loved the animation but also wanted to see some live action shots. We didn't have the time or resources for a full shoot, so AI became super helpful in generating a few shots."

records.description: Therese Detje, co-founder/CD at Zünc Studio in London: "Hublot celebrated a milestone year in 2025, the 20th anniversary of their iconic Big Bang watch. "They were planning a big showcase at the annual Watches & Wonders convention held in Geneva, and asked us to create a hero film and other deliverables for their larger global campaign as well. "The brief itself was open, with no storyboard or styleframes to start from, which is the kind of creative challenge we love. "It means we can explore various routes, try new techniques, test out different edits and moods, and surprise the client with a rich selection of R&D to discuss and develop further. "So we had a lot of freedom, as long as we covered a few important starting points: outer space (including a literal Big Bang), conceptualizing material innovation in a lab world, and introducing five new timepieces for the limited anniversary editions. "The trickiest part was distilling a lot of ideas, worlds, and watches into one cohesive film. We were careful not to make a film that was simply a montage of cool-looking shots. "It took many, many different edits for us to find the right flow of the film, to make sure we had a continuous story that made sense. "Especially since we had two worlds, the cosmos and the laboratory, it was really fun to figure out how on earth (ha!) we could design seamless transitions between them. "I think it really helps that we're a small and nimble team who all work in-house in our London studio. "We were constantly going over to each other's desks to discuss new edits and transitions, describing the motion with our own sound effects and gestures. "It helped us come up with new shot ideas, and ditch the ones that weren't working. That's how you get those money shots - the moments that make people stop and go ‘whoa, what was that?' "The watches didn't exist physically when we started. We got our first reference photos of the actual product three days before our delivery. So, we worked from the CAD files, material guides, and a lot of back and forth with Hublot's product manager. "To get the models looking absolutely hyper-real, there was a lot of nuance in the shaders we built, for example, dialing in exactly how deep and in what direction the brushed grain should go on metal parts. "It was our first watch project, and let me tell you that these products are way more complicated than any car models that we've worked on in the past. "One technical challenge was keeping the watch asset optimized. With 730+ parts, each with its own texture and microbevel, we had to be smart with keeping file sizes down to minimize loading times and keep render times as efficient as possible. "We worked mainly in Cinema 4D with Octane render, with a little bit of help from Houdini for some simulations. We edited in After Effects, where we also did comping and color grading." Schedule: Eight weeks.

raw_source.description: Therese Detje, co-founder/CD at Zünc Studio in London: "Hublot celebrated a milestone year in 2025, the 20th anniversary of their iconic Big Bang watch. "They were planning a big showcase at the annual Watches & Wonders convention held in Geneva, and asked us to create a hero film and other deliverables for their larger global campaign as well. "The brief itself was open, with no storyboard or styleframes to start from, which is the kind of creative challenge we love. "It means we can explore various routes, try new techniques, test out different edits and moods, and surprise the client with a rich selection of R&D to discuss and develop further. "So we had a lot of freedom, as long as we covered a few important starting points: outer space (including a literal Big Bang), conceptualizing material innovation in a lab world, and introducing five new timepieces for the limited anniversary editions. "The trickiest part was distilling a lot of ideas, worlds, and watches into one cohesive film. We were careful not to make a film that was simply a montage of cool-looking shots. "It took many, many different edits for us to find the right flow of the film, to make sure we had a continuous story that made sense. "Especially since we had two worlds, the cosmos and the laboratory, it was really fun to figure out how on earth (ha!) we could design seamless transitions between them. "I think it really helps that we're a small and nimble team who all work in-house in our London studio. "We were constantly going over to each other's desks to discuss new edits and transitions, describing the motion with our own sound effects and gestures. "It helped us come up with new shot ideas, and ditch the ones that weren't working. That's how you get those money shots - the moments that make people stop and go ‘whoa, what was that?' "The watches didn't exist physically when we started. We got our first reference photos of the actual product three days before our delivery. So, we worked from the CAD files, material guides, and a lot of back and forth with Hublot's product manager. "To get the models looking absolutely hyper-real, there was a lot of nuance in the shaders we built, for example, dialing in exactly how deep and in what direction the brushed grain should go on metal parts. "It was our first watch project, and let me tell you that these products are way more complicated than any car models that we've worked on in the past. "One technical challenge was keeping the watch asset optimized. With 730+ parts, each with its own texture and microbevel, we had to be smart with keeping file sizes down to minimize loading times and keep render times as efficient as possible. "We worked mainly in Cinema 4D with Octane render, with a little bit of help from Houdini for some simulations. We edited in After Effects, where we also did comping and color grading." Schedule: Eight weeks.

records.description: Chapman Bullock, CD/founder at Proper in Austin, Texas: "Our first brief from the client read ‘For the first time ever, AG1 will be available in flavored alternatives including Tropical, Berry, and Citrus. How do we represent these flavors visually?' "One of the creative challenges was ensuring viewers didn't assume each AG1 flavor was a different colored drink. AG1 is always the same signature green. "To emphasize this, we made the clear bottle filled with the green beverage the visual hero as it moved through various scenes—reinforcing that the color remains consistent across all flavors. "Since the bottle is in constant motion, this introduced a technical challenge with how the CG fluid behaved. Edu and Diego did an excellent job planning for this, making sure the contents inside the bottle reacted in a natural and realistic way. "We ended up using four different fluid simulations. In certain cases, we took the approach of simulating the liquid in a static bottle and adjusting the direction of gravity to control the motion. "This technique allowed us to repurpose a single sim across multiple shots, streamlining the process without sacrificing realism." "In addition to social and YouTube platforms, the film is also airing on broadcast TV. The client also extracted 4K stills from the project for use in billboards and print. " Schedule: Two months. Two to three weeks for design and R&D, six weeks for animation.

records.description: Javier Vallejo García, founder/CD at JVG in Madrid: "The client asked us to create a visually stunning commercial that conveyed the luxurious and indulgent essence of their Galaxy chocolate. "The brief emphasized sculptural elegance and a sense of artistic craftsmanship, highlighting the luxury aspect. "As this was a director's cut, the main challenge was finding a balance between creating something that truly resonated with us while remaining faithful to the original piece. "Striking that balance is never easy. In this case, we chose to move away from the heavy use of gold present in the original version and opted instead for a cleaner visual language. "This was paired with an original audio track, which, as usual, we produced entirely in-house. "On the technical side, the challenge was again about balance: we wanted to explore new creative solutions without overcomplicating the production in ways that would significantly delay publication. "We used simulations at several points, but in a measured way, enough to add impact and sophistication while ensuring the project remained streamlined and didn't take focus away from the next commercial production on our slate. "We approached the chocolate as if it were a sculpture in a museum. The goal was to elevate a familiar product into an artistic and almost surreal experience, turning everyday indulgence into something iconic. "In the end, we achieved a result that emphasized both innovation and luxury, which perfectly aligned with the brand's vision." Schedule: Eight weeks.

records.description: Joseph Clark, executive director at Oh Studio in London: "Our pals at agency Hope&Glory got in contact with a dream brief – to make a cute animated video to a track made by Tin Sounds, the wonderful minds behind the ‘Hey Duggee' music. "The biggest challenge was the timeline. We had two weeks and when deadlines are that tight you really have to fight the urge to just dive head first and have a little ice in the belly, as we Swedes say. "We actually started the project before having any music or lyrics, which meant we had to be clever with everything from resourcing and animation style to how we could build the narrative. "Knowing that we needed to design a cast of characters, this was the one thing we could begin developing. "I wanted all the kids to have their own personalities and quirks, from Jose the gentle soul to Mei and her cheeky antics, offering us some great stepping stones to build our scenes around. "Two weeks for a nearly two minute clip is pretty insane. Fortunately we could pull together a really sensational team, and once that was in place I knew we'd be able to make something we'd be really proud of. "Designing directly into after effects was a huge time saver. Along with the choice to animate at 8 fps or ‘on threes' gave it a charmingly choppy aesthetic whilst also speeding up the whole animation process! "Working with clients who are truly excited about creativity and craft is always an incredible joy for me as a director and the team making the magic."

records.description: Darren Price, ECD at Mighty Nice in Sydney: "This film is all about the creative process. In this instance 'the idea' is born in the shower and then grows, gets inspired, meets some challenges and then ultimately keeps on pushing forward. "The creative brief from the agency was to create a multimedia art direction which changed style, rendering and texturing in every scene - as the idea evolves and develops." "The client had a big vision that we loved, but it took the full bag of tricks to bring it to life." "The nature of the spot - an ever-changing journey with a central character, seemed like a great opportunity to experiment with new tools and techniques. "The first solution the team came up with was to use image cards and projection mapping to create depth without full 3D builds. Mike Lomas, head of studio: "Using our initial sketches, AI was then used in some of the more photo-real scenes to generate background images. These were then projection-mapped as a major workflow accelerator. " It was interesting to see which styles AI worked well for and then which it wasn't suitable for at all, such as the cloud scene. A shallow depth of field was deliberately chosen to blur the backgrounds and reduce the need for high-detail assets. "The character was animated traditionally, but we kept the movement to a horizontal path up until the final scene which really helped with scene building. "One of the biggest challenges turned out to be one of the most foundational animation challenges: the character walk cycle. "Our hero character is the letter R, and finding the right way for it to walk took the most R&D as our animators finally found a walk cycle that gave Roamy a full range of motion while preserving the logo's side-on R shape." Darren Price: "The biggest highlight of the project is that it was one of those rare ones that brought everyone in the studio together, 2D, 3D, design and Jason, our in-house IT specialist, got to flex their chops. "It also fosters a fun and collaborative creative environment, which is what running an animation studio is really all about."

records.description: Bristol-based illustrator/animator Con McHugh combines forces with digital design studio TwoMuch to add a little attitude to ON's premium marathon running shoe, the Cloudboom Max. Con McHugh: "Internally, ON had been playing with the shoe itself being this likeable, friendly character with sketched-on arms. "The campaign would be led by a 60-second video where Max would introduce himself and demonstrate all his cool tech. "The creative team at ON had a voice over scripted and some reference images. They had a huge amount of trust in letting me explore how we'd animate this character — not just what he was doing, but what he looked like and how he moved. "Drawing hands is, for many illustrators, their Achilles' heel, they avoid drawing hands and feet at all costs. "Of course, when ON approached me, this went round and round in my head, ‘This is hands, Conor — you'll be specifically drawing 60 seconds' worth of hands'. "We looked at floating hands (Rayman style), gloved hands (a la Mickey Mouse), we looked at the nature of how they moved. "The final style was a loving mix: thick and bouncy, a bit squishy, and drawn with just enough naivety to feel like street art, or something torn from my sketchbook. "The next stages of the project played out like this: storyboard, then a super rough animatic, which I passed to TwoMuch to whip up into an incredible 3D render. "It was a bit like tennis from then on — they'd send it back to me, I'd do some tests, suggest pacing tweaks, then back again — until we had something perfectly timed to the voice over and ready for the frame-by-frame animation. "I spent days locked into a routine, working from morning ‘til midnight. Maybe a sandwich, or a quick stroll round Bristol Harbor — just enough to stop me hallucinating arms on everything I looked at. "When it finally got to the stage where we combined the 3D, 2D, and TwoMuch's sound design — it was magic."

records.description: CD Miguel Rato​ and the CG specialists at Steelworks team with live action production duo Rebecca and Kevin Joelson for this dreamy take on comfort and sleep for luxury bedding brand Boll & Branch. ECD Chago Venable at Steelworks: "We collaborated closely with The Joelsons' live-action team to help shape a warm, inviting visual world, enhancing beautifully shot footage with animated CGI floral elements that evoke softness, growth, and seasonal renewal. "The client version was tailored to meet the campaign's commercial needs, while our director's cut expands on the original with extended floral animation, refined pacing, and a more immersive tone that showcases the expressive potential of CGI. "During the pre-shoot R&D phase, we used fully CGI-built rooms to explore lighting, composition, and styling. This helped to visualize the tone and pacing of the final film before the cameras rolled. "These virtual sets allowed us to test ideas, align creative direction, and ensure a seamless transition between the live-action shoot and the final integrated visuals. "By taking ownership of how live-action and CG would work together, we ensured the footage was captured with precision, resulting in a cohesive, elevated final film where practical and digital elements feel naturally unified." "To bring the concept of natural renewal to life, our team conducted extensive R&D focused on the behavior and choreography of blooming flowers. "We studied time-lapse photography, growth patterns, and petal mechanics to develop animations that felt both organic and elevated. "Building on our blooming animation system, we developed a layered choreography of movement throughout the film. "Each flower's growth served as the foundation for additional motion, petals unfurling into light, stems weaving gently through the space, and floral clusters cascading in carefully timed waves. "In the early stages of the project, we used AI tools to rapidly explore visual directions and floral compositions. "These generative references helped us iterate quickly on mood, form, and spatial arrangement, which provided a creative springboard before entering full 3D production. "Our team led the creative and visual direction for the live-talent shoot, shaping key decisions around framing, lighting, and set design to ensure every moment aligned with our planned CGI integration. "By taking ownership of how live-action and CG would work together, we ensured the footage was captured with precision, resulting in a cohesive, elevated final film where practical and digital elements feel naturally unified."

records.description: Andreas Ibsen, CD, and Thomas Bay, co-founder at Frame in Copenhagen: "Swiss furniture manufacturer USM asked us to introduce their new magnetic panels without focusing on specific configurations, locations, or situations. "The goal was to highlight the product itself, leading us to design a non-sensical megastructure built from the USM Haller system. "This construction provided the framework for showcasing the panels' colors, functions, and design options while enabling playful compositions and dynamic movement. "The film also needed to align with the client's vision for the product launch at the Salone del Mobile trade show in Milan. "The biggest creative challenge was balancing the various elements: the furniture components, the oversized megastructure, the vibrant color palette, and the sunny, blue-sky aesthetic. "The megastructure inherently introduced a sense of chaos, and instead of fighting it, we leaned into that madness. "Our creative approach emphasized options, multiplicity, fun, and creativity — very much in line with the client's emphasis on "playful." "Another creative priority was introducing fabric as a new material in the USM Haller system. "We started with free-flowing textile to communicate tactility, then contrasted it with solid metal, ending with the ball joints shaping the final magnetic panels. "The technical challenge was to ensure accuracy at every scale and camera angle while handling the complexity of the megastructure. "We avoided using multiple levels of detail to keep the workflow consistent, which gave us complete freedom during R&D without risking inaccuracies. "To solve this, we built a USM Haller system builder HDA where each module existed as its own node. This allowed us to manipulate and animate individual modules while preserving the procedural integrity of the larger system. "For efficiency, Redshift proxies were used for most geometry, with rods generated procedurally through sweeps and curves. This setup ensured real-time viewport playback and fast rendering." Schedule: Seven weeks.

records.description: Virgile Machala and Maria Markova, producers at Eddy in Paris: "Van Rysel needed a bold, unconventional film to launch their new RCR-F INFERNO capsule, a line of high-performance cycling gear. "The goal was double: present their most advanced bike in action, and deliver a sensory, visceral experience that would resonate with cyclists. "Instead of following traditional premium codes, they asked for something more instinctive, more physical, something that could embody speed, pressure, and obsession. "The brief left a lot of room for interpretation, which allowed us to build a metaphorical, immersive vision of Hell, seen from inside a rider's mind. "The main challenge was to find the right balance between narrative ambition and raw emotional impact. "We wanted to convey both the technical precision of elite cycling and the trance-like state of exhaustion athletes experience in competition. "Animation gave us the freedom to push the sensory sliders: speed lines, distortion, visual repetition, metaphorical creatures like Cerberus or serpents, we crafted a hallucinated final lap. "We built the entire film around a single, continuous shot, a dynamic, flowing camera that never stops moving around the rider. "This meant coordinating angles, transitions, and scaling in a seamless way, all while preserving rhythm and clarity. "The animation itself was intentionally raw: expressive drawings, a restricted palette (black, red, orange, grey, white), and grainy textures helped us go fast and stay coherent with the tone. "Every element—visual or sound—had to serve the physicality and tension of the ride. "The project was completed in less than two months. From writing and storyboarding to animation, compositing, and sound, everything moved at a high pace. "The urgency matched the film's subject: a hypnotic sprint, built in the same energy. We embraced a flexible, collaborative rhythm—progressing on all fronts simultaneously, with constant dialogue between the director, artists, and the Van Rysel team. "For animation, we primarily used Adobe Animate and After Effects. This setup allowed for a fast and flexible workflow, well-suited to the expressive, textured aesthetic we were aiming for. "Sound design was crafted by Sodasound, who worked closely with us to create an immersive, narrative audio track centered on breathing, wind, and mechanical tension. "We used minimal music—most of the storytelling comes from the soundscape and a voice-over that feels like a devilish coach inside the rider's head." Schedule: Two months.

records.description: Andreas Wanda, founder and VFX supervisor at Atmos Studios in Sydney, Australia: "The director Yianni Warnock said he wanted this spot to be epic. "Over several days, the conversation went something like this… Yianni: We need cars, hundreds of cars, as far as the eye can see. And we need an ice cream truck – lots of them, wait, we found an ice cream truck, but can you do a house? Andreas: Yes Yianni: There's going to be a car on two wheels. Andreas: What? Yianni: It'll be split in half. Andreas: So, you want us to build a splitting car? Yianni: No, we're building that practically, but can you paint out the rig? Andreas: Right! Yianni: And there's a wide birds-eye view of a spectacle of cars at the end. We'll have about 20 cars for the shoot. Andreas: Ok. So we're doing a mix of split-screen practical cars and augmenting with CG cars. How many cars? Yianni: 100, maybe 200 max. Andreas: Ok.. Let's go! "Rendering a CG car isn't hard these days. Adding steering and suspension to that car gets a little trickier - something I was determined to achieve to get those flickering reflections as they travelled over the rough terrain. "Simulating and rendering hundreds of cars travelling over this rough terrain isn't a feature available in your off-the-shelf software packages. "It was clear we needed to do a ton of R&D on this just to be able to execute it. "We had a system that was so efficient in the end that when a request was made to change the layout, it wasn't an issue. In the end, we rendered about 4000 cars. "The biggest creative challenge was ‘creating cars as far as the eye could see' and making them move and look like real cars. Then we added drivers to each one. It was all done on PC's with high-end GPUs – we needed the VRAM to be able to process the volume of geometry that was thrown at them. "Software-wise, we used Maya, Houdini, Redshift, and a few other bits and pieces. To tie it all together, we created a bespoke pipeline that could translate elements from one package to another, distributing car types and color assignments randomly based on user-defined percentage values for each color. "I really must hand it to the compositors at ARC. They did an amazing job, not only replacing skies, cutting and pasting a mixture of live action and CG cars throughout, but cleaning up the sodden ground covered in muddy tire marks from end to end." Schedule: 10 weeks.

records.description: Denis Danin, head of studio/art director at Innerlights in Yerevan, Armenia: "The project was created for Milan Design Week, where Spanish automotive brand Cupra was unveiling several new products. "We were invited to produce a film that would spotlight their new 3D-printed sneaker, developed in collaboration with Zellerfeld. The goal was to showcase the sneaker's design and its connection to Cupra's aesthetic. "The brief included two main directives. First, we needed to open by showcasing the car capsule, then transition into the sneaker, showing how it's printed. "Second, we had to highlight the parametric design elements shared by both the car and the sneaker, visually drawing a connection between the two products. "The biggest creative challenge was developing that concept and storyline to unify the different worlds of the car and the sneaker, both visually and narratively. "We needed an element that would not only tie these two products together within the same universe, but also serve a functional purpose. "That's where the idea of lasers came in. Futuristic, sleek, and technological, just like Cupra and Zellerfeld, the lasers became a key visual bridge between the products. "They helped us guide the viewer's eye, emphasize the shared parametric design details, and introduce the brand's signature copper color. "The lasers essentially became the third character in the story, scanning the space, analyzing the surfaces, printing the sneaker, and creating a seamless flow between two otherwise unrelated objects. "We had a week for developing the concept and three weeks for production. The deadline was non-negotiable due to the live event in Milan, so we had to keep a tight and focused workflow."

records.description: Tom Raynor, CD at UNTOLD Studios in London: "We were tasked with an incredibly exciting brief: to showcase the remarkable capabilities of the new Heart of Joy control unit in the latest BMW Neue Klasse range. "This groundbreaking technology unifies all driving functions into a single unit, enabling significantly faster, more precise, and more efficient control. "The challenge became even more intriguing when we learned we'd need to illustrate this using the analogy of an octopus dancing a waltz. "This was, without a doubt, one of our most ambitious animation projects to date, and from the outset, we knew this would be a wild, creative ride. "We began with extensive animation R&D, exploring how to reinterpret human dance movements for a character with eight limbs. "Initially, we aimed to preserve as much authentic octopus behaviour as possible. However, we quickly realised this made the performance come across as creepy rather than fun and entertaining. "To strike the right tone, we gradually dialled up the human qualities, retaining just a hint of cephalopod charm. That shift brought the performance to life with the comedic flair we were after. "Midway through, the request came in for the octopus to moonwalk, pushing the absurdity and the fun even further. "One of the major technical challenges was the underwater environment. On the shoot days, the conditions were less than ideal. Murky water and heavy particulates made for very low visibility. "Our compositing team rose to the occasion, developing clever techniques to clean up the footage. "They removed floating debris and enhanced clarity, transforming the raw plates into something that felt straight out of a Planet Earth documentary. "The project was awarded at the end of January, leaving us just over two weeks before the shoot to get everything organized. "We worked closely with the director and the shoot team, creating previs cameras to explore shot framing and basic animations to help map out the action - all of which informed the choice of locations and underwater camera moves. "From edit lock, we had roughly 12 weeks to complete post-production. This proved challenging, as crafting the perfect edit took time, and the waltz animation was closely tied to the music, which continued to evolve well into the animation process. "At Untold, we use Maya for modeling, rigging, and animation, alongside ZBrush and Substance for sculpting and texturing. "For lighting, look development, character FX, FX, and rendering, we rely on Houdini. All compositing is handled in Nuke."

records.description: Erwin Charrier, director at Pleix in Paris: "Moët & Chandon tasked us with translating the concept of 'Haute Œnologie' into a 30-second journey. "Drawing inspiration from the refined elegance of high fashion jewelry, we explored and developed various creative directions before distilling them into the final concept. "We envisioned luxurious, microscopic worlds where dancing bubbles transform into crystalline forms, ultimately revealing the iconic bottle and celebrating the spirit of the Collection Impériale. "The first challenge was to come up with an idea that instantly evokes high fashion jewelry, haute couture, and champagne. The second was finding the right visual style. "Real bubbles are very complex visually, and we didn't want to fall into a world that was too macro-photographic and concrete and also wanted to avoid it looking too much like CG liquid. "Luxury is about dreams and desire, often interpreted in an abstract, arty, and minimalist way. So, we chose a metaphorical representation of champagne bubbles. "Our client liked the research we did with Midjourney, and the first challenge was to replicate this very pure look without looking too perfect, as CGI can often be. "So we developed a system of 3D prisms in front of the 3D camera, adding a more natural look and micro-flares, as if shot through an old lens. "DOPs use the same principle on shoots when they want a more natural image that flares in the highlights. There are 2D plugins that do this badly, and we tested a brute-force approach for the first time. "Animation was also an interesting task, as we had to find the right balance between organic yet simple movements to maintain a certain purity. "At first, we experimented with highly complex particle systems and fluid dynamics, before finally going to very simple, hand-made choreographies. "Moët & Chandon approached us directly, which meant we first had to develop a concept before moving forward with the film. "It took about two months of R&D and key visual development before the idea and storyboard were approved and a total of four months to complete the final delivery. "The first music video we directed was for Plaid, so it was a real pleasure to collaborate with them and Warp Records once again on the soundtrack for this project. The music played a crucial role in bringing the film to life."

Instead of positioning an Airbnb on an empty stage where the focus is on the home itself, this Airbnb is nestled into a full-frame, immersive forest. records.description: Dominik Bochenski, founder /CD at Tantrum Studio in Toronto: "The production company approached us about the feasibility of digitally recreating Canadian cancer research activist Terry Fox's face and seamlessly compositing it onto an actor. "Initially, there was discussion about a more traditional multi-angle, cut-heavy edit that would gradually reveal Terry's face. "But as the concept developed, it became clear that the spot would be a single, continuous take – meaning there would be no room to hide imperfections. "Because there were only a handful of grainy photos of Terry Fox, an AI-driven face swap would not deliver the level of realism required for the film. "After extensive research and conversations, it became clear that the only viable approach was a fully CG solution. "We needed to model, texture, shade, track, animate, light, render, and composite Terry's face from scratch. "The biggest creative challenge was twofold. First, making a believable CG human is still one of the hardest things to do in VFX. The tiniest imperfections in proportions, skin texture, or lighting can break the illusion. "The second major challenge was staying true to Terry's likeness. As Canadians, we all have a mental image of him, but even real photos of him sometimes felt inconsistent. "On top of that, we were sharing our work with the Terry Fox Foundation and his family, which made the stakes even higher. It had to feel like Terry, not just a CG version of him. The first technical challenge was that without a scan of Terry's head, determining his true shape was a guessing game. "We sculpted in ZBrush using key reference images, and at times, we felt confident that we were on the right track. "But as soon as we moved the model into our Maya scene with the correct lens and lighting, everything changed. "He would look completely different – sometimes shockingly so. We had to rely on trial, error, and pure intuition, often making intentional exaggerations just to have it feel right in-camera. "The second technical challenge was matching the CG Terry to the real actors standing all around him. "This wasn't just about making the CG head look real – it had to integrate seamlessly with the live-action footage, where the lighting and skin response were naturally perfect. "Our actor served as a strong reference for integration, but he looked nothing like Terry and was noticeably older, which affected the way light interacted with his face. "We had to constantly tweak the shading, rendering and compositing, often by gut instinct, to ensure the CG Terry didn't feel separate from the scene. "Tracking was another major hurdle. We brought in a specialist to refine the tracking, but Adam's facial proportions were different from Terry's, so we also had to subtly warp the footage to make everything align properly. "Rendering also became a challenge due to the length of the shot. Running full renders often took an entire day, and evaluating only partial sections didn't give us the full picture. "To judge realism, we needed to process the entire sequence properly, play it back, and then assess what was working and what wasn't. It was an exhausting but necessary process. "In the end, we did incorporate AI-based face swapping, but only as a fine-tuning tool, which was trained not on top of the footage but rather on our intermediate CG composite. "The face swap systems that provided any sort of usable results looked very fake, but we found that mixing these in just around the eyes helped refine the likeness. It wasn't a replacement for our CG work, but rather an enhancement. "This project was a reality check for anyone who thinks AI is a magic bullet. While AI-generated imagery can be effective in some contexts, it often falls apart under real production demands. "We experimented heavily with deepfake approaches, but they simply weren't robust enough to hold up in a high-end cinematic setting. The moment you need full creative control, you quickly realize that traditional VFX techniques are still the backbone of this kind of work."

"These shots echo the designer's attention to detail and are interwoven with high-energy riding sequences (also built in CG) that showcase the motorcycle's beauty and rideability. "This approach allowed us to showcase Eccles' visionary design and served as a fitting way to announce ‘a new era in motorcycling'. "To achieve this, we brought the concept of ‘Genesis' to life in the physical sense (how materials and components come together) and in the conceptual sense (the evolution of motorcycle design). "The story structure not only mirrors the design process, but represents the fundamental shift from combustion to electric power and XP's position as a vanguard of that transformation."

records.description: Colle Ignacio Godoy, EP at BUDA.tv in Buenos Aires: "The idea was to bring Vear, a character created by Japanese artist Verdy, to life for the Beats headphones. "The result was a series of pieces in which Beats and Verdy join forces in a collaboration that seamlessly blends music, urban culture, and avant-garde design. A perfect expression of the Beats spirit. "One of the biggest challenges we faced was translating Vear, a 2D character full of Verdy's signature gestures, attitude and street energy, into a 3D being that could exist convincingly in a rich, tangible world. "It wasn't just about modeling or texturing. It was about preserving his essence, the looseness of the line, the emotion in each pose and making sure that once he stepped into three dimensions, he still felt alive, touchable and undeniably Verdy. "Every detail, from his proportions to the way light interacts with his materials, was crafted to keep that balance between animation and reality, design and soul. "The production timeline spanned 12 weeks, covering the development of both the teaser and the first spot. "The response from Verdy's team was overwhelmingly positive. They embraced the character, the story and the visual style from the very beginning. "That enthusiasm fueled the entire process, keeping the energy high and pushing everyone involved to keep raising the bar until we reached the finish line. "The overall production was handled in Blender, which served as the backbone for layout, modeling, and rendering. Maya was used for animation. Meanwhile, all graphic design and compositing were developed within Adobe Creative Suite."

records.description: Simon Ravet, director at I-REEL in Paris: "We have collaborated for over eight years with the Ulysse Nardin team, and each project is a really creative time, always inspiring and innovative, offering lots of freedom for creativity. "They wanted to introduce their new product, the Diver [AIR], and its major features: high technology, high horology, high performance. "The brief was to create a link with the Watches & Wonders trade show booth scenography already engaged when we started, so we imagined a scientific experimentation laboratory located in the Swiss mountains. "To echo the watch that weighs only 52g, we focused on evoking a sense of lightness and aimed to convey this notion throughout the film. "We drew inspiration from inflatable architecture for the design of the laboratory, which brings up a sense of protection and shock resistance, mirroring the watch's features and creating a harmonious blend of form and function. "This inflated laboratory is a white, minimalist, and futuristic place whose organic shapes blend into the snowy natural landscape of the Swiss Jura. "To add a human dimension, we incorporated AI-generated sequences showing athletes undergoing tests, pushing their watches to the same limits as themselves. "These animations required a lot of reworking within our traditional VFX pipeline to achieve the level of quality we were aiming for. "As usual, the schedule was quite tight since we had less than two months between the brief and the delivery. "We spent two weeks developing the creative concept and finally proposed two different directions. When one was approved by the client, we spent two weeks working on the animatic and around three weeks on CGI texturing and rendering."
